subject: English Language
summary: Covers the grammar rules behind error spotting, sentence improvement and fill-in-the-blank questions: subject-verb agreement, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs and conjunctions, tenses, articles, prepositions, question tags, and the transformation rules for active-passive voice and direct-indirect speech. These rules decide a large share of the English marks in DSSSB papers, and each question usually tests exactly one of them.

sections.heading: Subject-verb agreement
sections.body:
The verb agrees with the **real subject** in number. - Two subjects joined by **and** take a plural verb, unless they name one person or idea: "The secretary and treasurer **has** arrived" (one person); "Bread and butter **is** my breakfast".
- **Each, every, either, neither, everyone, somebody, nobody** take a singular verb: "Each of the boys **has** a book."
- **Either … or / neither … nor**: the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject: "Neither the teacher nor the students **were** present."
- **as well as, along with, together with, besides, with**: the verb agrees with the **first** subject: "The captain, along with his players, **was** praised."
- **The number of** + singular verb; **a number of** + plural verb.
- **One of the** + plural noun + singular verb: "One of my friends **has** gone abroad."
- **Collective nouns** take a singular verb when the group acts as one unit ("The jury **has** given its verdict") and a plural verb when members act separately ("The jury **were** divided").
- Always plural: scissors, trousers, spectacles, cattle, police (as a body of people). Singular despite -s: news, mathematics, measles. **Many a** + singular noun takes a singular verb. Uncountable nouns have no plural: information, advice, furniture, luggage, equipment.

sections.heading: Pronouns, adjectives, adverbs and conjunctions
sections.body:
**Pronouns**
- Object form after prepositions: "between you and **me**" (not I).
- After than/as, use the form the full clause needs: "He is taller than **I** (am)."
- Some verbs take a reflexive object: avail **oneself** of, absent **oneself** from, enjoy **ourselves**.

**Adjectives**
- No double comparison: "more better" ✗ → "better".
- **superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior, preferable** take **to**, not than.
- **elder/eldest** for family members (not followed by than); **older** for general comparison with than.
- **fewer** with countable nouns (fewer mistakes), **less** with uncountable (less water).
- **farther** for physical distance; **further** also means additional.

**Adverbs and conjunctions** (fixed pairs)
- **Hardly / scarcely … when**; **no sooner … than**: "No sooner had he left than it rained."
- **Not only … but also**, **either … or**, **neither … nor**, **both … and** (not both … as well as).
- **Lest** takes **should** (or the base form), never not: "Walk carefully lest you **should** fall."
- **Unless** is already negative: "Unless you work hard, you will fail" (not "unless you do not").

sections.heading: Sentence improvement: idiom, parallelism and redundancy
sections.body:
Find the rule the underlined part breaks and choose the shortest option that fixes it. Common fixes:
- **Parallel structure**: items joined by and/or, or by paired conjunctions, must have the same form. "She likes reading, writing and **to swim**" → "and swimming".
- **Conditionals**: If + present → will; If + past → would; If + had + past participle → would have + past participle. "If I **had known**, I would have helped." Use "If I **were** you" for unreal situations.
- **Redundancy**: remove words that repeat the meaning: "return back", "repeat again", "revert back", "each and every", "the reason is because" (use "the reason is that").
- **Wrong word forms**: "discuss about" → "discuss"; "reach at" → "reach"; "resemble with" → "resemble"; "enter into the room" → "enter the room".
- **It is time / it is high time** + past tense: "It is high time we **left**."
- **Dangling modifiers**: "Walking down the road, a tree fell" → "As I was walking down the road, a tree fell."

sections.heading: Fill in the blanks and question tags
sections.body:
Fill-in-the-blank questions test collocations (which preposition or word naturally follows), tense, articles, conjunctions and question tags.

**Question tags**
- Positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag: "You can swim, **can't you**?" "She doesn't eat meat, **does she**?"
- Use the same auxiliary; with no auxiliary use do/does/did: "He went home, **didn't he**?"
- "I am …" → **aren't I**? "Let's go" → **shall we**? Imperatives → **will you**? ("Close the door, will you?")
- Words like **hardly, scarcely, seldom, never, nobody, nothing** make the statement negative → positive tag: "He hardly works, **does he**?"
- **Everyone/somebody/nobody** → tag with **they**: "Everyone was there, weren't they?"

**Clue words for tense**: since/for → perfect tense; yesterday/ago/last year → simple past; already/yet/just → present perfect; by the time (past) → past perfect.

sections.heading: Tenses
sections.body:
Key rules tested in error-spotting:
- **Present perfect** is never used with a definite past time: "I have seen him yesterday" ✗ → "I saw him yesterday".
- **Since** + point of time, **for** + period: "She has lived here since 2015 / for ten years."
- **Stative verbs** (know, believe, understand, love, like, own, belong, seem, contain) are not used in continuous forms: "I am knowing" ✗ → "I know".
- In **time and condition clauses** (when, before, after, until, as soon as, if), use the present for a future meaning: "I will call you when he **comes**" (not "will come").
- For two past actions, the earlier one takes the **past perfect**: "The train **had left** before we reached the station."

sections.heading: Articles
Prepositions
sections.body:
**Time**: **at** for an exact time (at 6 pm, at night, at noon); **on** for days and dates (on Monday, on 15 August); **in** for months, years, seasons and parts of the day (in May, in 2020, in winter, in the morning).

**Place**: **at** a point (at the gate), **in** an enclosed or large area (in the room, in Delhi), **on** a surface (on the table). **Into** shows movement inward ("He jumped into the river").

**Pairs**: **between** two, **among** more than two; **beside** = next to, **besides** = in addition to; **since** = from a point of time, **for** = a period.

Many verbs and adjectives take fixed prepositions (see table). Some verbs take **no** preposition: discuss, reach, enter, resemble, order, attack, comprise ("comprises three parts", not "comprises of").

sections.heading: Active and passive voice
sections.body:
To change active to passive: the **object becomes the subject**, the verb becomes **be (in the same tense) + past participle**, and the old subject goes after **by** (often dropped if unimportant). Pronouns change case: I → me, we → us, he → him, she → her, they → them.

- Only **transitive** verbs (with an object) have a passive form.
- Perfect continuous tenses are normally not changed into passive.
- **Imperatives**: "Open the window." → "Let the window be opened." Requests: "Please help me." → "You are requested to help me."
- **Questions**: "Did she write the letter?" → "Was the letter written by her?" "Who broke the glass?" → "By whom was the glass broken?"
- **Prepositional verbs** keep their preposition: "They laughed at him." → "He was laughed at by them."
- Some passives take other prepositions: known **to**, pleased **with**, surprised **at**, filled **with**, interested **in**.

sections.heading: Direct and indirect speech (narration)
sections.body:
**When the reporting verb is in the past** (said, told), the tense of the reported speech moves one step back.

**Pronouns (SON rule)**: first person changes according to the **S**ubject of the reporting verb, second person according to the **O**bject, third person **N**o change.

**Sentence types**
- Statements: said to → **told**; connector **that**.
- Yes/no questions: said to → **asked**; connector **if/whether**; question becomes statement order: He said to her, "Have you finished?" → He asked her **if she had finished**.
- Wh-questions: the wh-word is the connector: He said to me, "Where do you live?" → He asked me **where I lived**.
- Commands and requests: **ordered/told/requested/advised** + **to**-infinitive (negative: **not to**): She said to him, "Don't shout." → She told him **not to shout**.
- Exclamations: **exclaimed with joy/sorrow/surprise** that …
- Proposals with let's: **suggested that** they **should** …

**No tense change** when the reporting verb is in the present or future ("He says that he is tired"), or when the reported speech is a **universal truth** or habitual fact.

**Time and place words**: now → then; today → that day; tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the previous day; ago → before; here → there; this → that; these → those; last night → the previous night; next week → the following week.

workedExamples.problem: Spot the error: Neither the principal nor the teachers (1)/ was present (2)/ at the annual function. (3)/ No error (4)
workedExamples.solution:
With neither … nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "the teachers" (plural).
"was" should be "were". **Error in part (2)**.

workedExamples.problem: Improve the underlined part: Hardly had I reached the platform **than the train left**.
workedExamples.solution:
"Hardly" pairs with "when", not "than" (no sooner … than).
Correct: "Hardly had I reached the platform **when the train left**".

workedExamples.problem: Fill in the blank: She has been unwell ______ last Monday. (since / for / from / by)
workedExamples.solution: "Last Monday" is a point of time and the tense is present perfect continuous, so **since** is correct. "For" would need a period such as "for a week".

workedExamples.problem: Change into passive: The committee will announce the results tomorrow.
workedExamples.solution:
Object "the results" becomes the subject; future tense → will be + past participle.
**The results will be announced by the committee tomorrow.**

workedExamples.problem: Change into indirect speech: She said to me, "I am writing a letter now."
workedExamples.solution:
said to → told; I → she (subject of reporting verb); am writing → was writing; now → then.
**She told me that she was writing a letter then.**

workedExamples.problem: Change into indirect speech: The teacher said to the boys, "Do not make a noise."
workedExamples.solution:
A command: said to → told/ordered; negative → not to + base verb.
**The teacher told the boys not to make a noise.**

pitfalls: Making the verb agree with the noun nearest to it instead of the real subject ("The quality of the mangoes are good" ✗ → is).
Using a plural verb after each, every, either, neither or many a.
Using present perfect with a definite past time (yesterday, last year, in 2019).
Using 'than' after superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior or preferable.
Choosing a/an by the first letter instead of the first sound (a hour ✗, an university ✗).
Adding prepositions to discuss, reach, enter, resemble or comprise.
Changing a universal truth into the past tense in indirect speech.
Keeping question word order in indirect questions ("He asked where did I live" ✗).
quickRevision: Neither … nor / either … or: verb agrees with the nearer subject.
As well as / along with: verb agrees with the first subject.
The number of + singular; a number of + plural.
One of the + plural noun + singular verb.
Since + point of time; for + period.
When/if clauses use present tense for future meaning.
an hour, an MLA, a university, a European.
The Himalayas, the Ganga; but Mount Everest, Lake Superior.
Indirect speech: present → past, past → past perfect, will → would.
SON: 1st person → subject, 2nd → object, 3rd → no change.
Question tags: I am → aren't I; Let's → shall we; imperative → will you.
